preacher.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
preacher.role: Lutheran pastor, theologian, Confessing Church seminary director
preacher.bio: Dietrich Bonhoeffer (4 February 1906 – 9 April 1945), born in Breslau, was a German Lutheran pastor and theologian. He served as a pastoral assistant (Vikar) to the German-speaking congregation in Barcelona in 1928–29, spent 1930–31 at Union Theological Seminary in New York, and was ordained in November 1931 while lecturing at the University of Berlin and serving as student chaplain at the Technical College. After Hitler came to power he opposed the pro-Nazi 'German Christians'. He then served as pastor of two German-speaking congregations in London (October 1933 – April 1935) and directed the Confessing Church's illegal preachers' seminary at Finkenwalde until the Gestapo closed it in September 1937, after which he continued clandestine training of ordinands in Pomerania. He joined the German military intelligence service, within which his brother-in-law Hans von Dohnanyi belonged to a group secretly planning against Hitler. He was arrested on 5 April 1943, held in Tegel military prison, and hanged at Flossenbürg concentration camp on 9 April 1945. His prison letters were published after his death as Widerstand und Ergebung (1951; English: Letters and Papers from Prison).
preacher.corpus_note: Victoria J. Barnett, general editor of the English Dietrich Bonhoeffer Works, counts seventy-one complete sermons or homilies in the collected works, or more if Bible studies and the circular letters to his students are included. The critical German texts are in the Dietrich Bonhoeffer Werke (16 volumes plus an index volume; the sermons appear in the chronological volumes, e.g. vols. 10–15), and the English texts are in the 17-volume Dietrich Bonhoeffer Works (Fortress Press, 1996–2014). Isabel Best's Collected Sermons (2012) selects 31 of them, and Barnett's second volume (2017) adds 28 further sermons and meditations.

sermons.title: God Is with Us
sermons.occasion: Quasimodogeniti (first Sunday after Easter); preached as pastoral assistant (Vikar)
sermons.published_in: DBW 10, pp. 467–473 (German); English in DBWE 10 and The Collected Sermons of Dietrich Bonhoeffer, ed. Isabel Best (Fortress, 2012), pp. 1–6
sermons.summary: The sermon begins with old legends and the Eden story, where God walks among people. It argues that the Easter promise 'I am with you always' means God is near now, not only in a lost past. Christ is present in his word, which tells people at every stage of life both that God loves them and that God is holy and asks them to be holy. That nearness also brings judgment and responsibility, but grace comes with the judgment. Christ also meets people in every neighbour, such as the stranger, the beggar and the sick, so that human community becomes one of the ways God is revealed.
sermons.context: Bonhoeffer, then 22, preached this while serving as pastoral assistant to a German-speaking congregation in Barcelona as part of his training for ordination. Editor Isabel Best notes that he found preparing and delivering his first sermons challenging. It opens Best's 2012 selection, and the publisher offers it as a free sample chapter.

sermons.title: Staying Grounded in Turbulent Times (Sermon on 2 Chronicles 20:12)
sermons.date_text: 8 May 1932 (date marked uncertain by the German editors)
sermons.published_in: DBW 11, pp. 416–422 (German); English in DBWE 11 and The Collected Sermons of Dietrich Bonhoeffer, vol. 2, ed. Victoria J. Barnett (Fortress, 2017)
sermons.summary: The sermon takes up King Jehoshaphat's prayer, 'We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you'. It applies the prayer to hearers caught in the instability and competing worldviews of 1932 and directs them to look to God. According to a published review, like much of Bonhoeffer's preaching it points to God's mercy expressed in Christ's death on the cross.
sermons.context: Preached in Berlin in the last year of the Weimar Republic, when Bonhoeffer was a university lecturer and student chaplain at the Technical College in Berlin (Isabel Best). The critical German edition (DBW 11) dates it to Exaudi Sunday, 8 May 1932, but marks the date with a question mark.

sermons.title: The Things That Are Above (Sermon on Colossians 3:1–4)
sermons.published_in: DBW 11, pp. 444–453 (German); English in DBWE 11 and The Collected Sermons of Dietrich Bonhoeffer (2012), pp. 49–58
sermons.summary: Bonhoeffer asks whether Christians have the courage to show that their faith is not an opiate that leaves them content in the face of injustice. He criticises a church that trails decades behind the movements of history. He warns that the church may again be asked for martyrs' blood. Such blood, he says, would not be innocent like that of the first witnesses; it would carry the church's own guilt, the guilt of the unprofitable servant.
sermons.context: This is the second of two sermons on the same text, preached a week apart (12 and 19 June 1932, per DBW 11). German Wikipedia, citing DBW 11, p. 446, and the German theologian Jochen Teuffel both place this one in the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church.

sermons.title: … In the Eleventh Hour of Our Church (Sermon on Revelation 2:4–5, 7)
sermons.published_in: DBW 12, pp. 423–430 (German); English in DBWE 12 and The Collected Sermons of Dietrich Bonhoeffer, vol. 2 (2017)
sermons.summary: The sermon keeps repeating the charge in Revelation 2 that the church has abandoned the love it had at first. It contrasts triumphant Reformation celebrations, and the confident quoting of Luther's 'Here I stand', with the real state of German Protestantism, which it describes as losing its way. Bonhoeffer calls for letting Luther's memory rest so that the gospel can be heard again. He names the church's lack of prayer, love, grace and devotion, and ends by calling hearers to go and do the works they did at first.
sermons.context: Reviewer Kyle Jantzen calls it the most forceful of the few sermons in the second Collected Sermons volume that refer directly to church and state politics, and places it just after the November 1932 Reichstag election; DBW 12's date, 6 November 1932, is the day that election was held. It was preached less than three months before Hitler was appointed chancellor on 30 January 1933.

sermons.title: Overcoming Fear
sermons.occasion: Evening service on a Sunday after Epiphany (DBW 12 heads it '3rd Sunday after Epiphany'; Teuffel gives the 2nd)
sermons.published_in: DBW 12, pp. 439–446 (German); English in DBWE 12 and The Collected Sermons of Dietrich Bonhoeffer (2012), pp. 59–66
sermons.summary: Using the story of the storm on the lake, Bonhoeffer describes fear as a power that hollows people out from within and cuts them off from God and from one another. He speaks of the fear of the coming hour and days that grips people in Germany and in their own lives. He separates false security, which depends on calm circumstances, from faith that rests on God alone. He tells hearers that Christ is in the boat, and that the church's particular task is to keep proclaiming that fear has been overcome.
sermons.context: Preached in a time of economic and political crisis in Germany; Ryan Hoselton notes that unemployment had risen above six million. Hitler was appointed chancellor fifteen days later, on 30 January 1933.

sources.label: Ryan Hoselton, 'Bonhoeffer's Answer to Political Turmoil: Preach!', Christianity Today (May 2016)

sermons.title: Gideon: God Is My Lord
sermons.published_in: DBW 12, pp. 447–454 (German); English in DBWE 12 and The Collected Sermons of Dietrich Bonhoeffer (2012), pp. 67–74
sermons.summary: Retelling Gideon's call, Bonhoeffer stresses that God chooses a weak and doubting man and that God's promise to be with him is enough, without any other help. God's victory comes through faith, not human strength, and it humbles human pride. Gideon's refusal to become king ('the Lord will rule over you') becomes a claim that God alone is Lord, and the sermon ends by setting the cross over the world as the sign of that lordship.
sermons.context: Preached in Berlin four weeks after Hitler was appointed chancellor. Reviewer Barry Harvey (Christian Century) calls it the first sermon Bonhoeffer preached after Hitler came to power. He also says it set Gideon, who had to renounce power, honour and pride, against Siegfried, the Nibelung hero whom Nazi propaganda idealised.

sermons.title: Of Priests and Prophets in the New Germany (Sermon on Exodus 32)
sermons.published_in: DBW 12, pp. 459–464 (German); English in DBWE 12 and The Collected Sermons of Dietrich Bonhoeffer, vol. 2 (2017)
sermons.summary: Reading the golden calf story as a conflict between Aaron's 'church of the world' and Moses' church that waits on God, the sermon describes a church that wants a god it can see. That church will not wait, acts on its own initiative, and claims divine authority through its priesthood. Bonhoeffer counts his hearers as part of that idolatrous church. He declares that the cross puts an end to all idolatry, and speaks of a God who tolerates no other gods yet meets people with boundless forgiveness.
sermons.context: Preached in spring 1933, as democracy was being dismantled, the pro-Nazi 'German Christian' movement was rising, and the church struggle was beginning (Jantzen).

sources.label: Kyle Jantzen, review of Collected Sermons vol. 2, Contemporary Church History Quarterly (2018)
DBW 12 table of contents (Dietrich Bonhoeffer Portal)

sermons.title: Who Do You Say That I Am?
sermons.occasion: Sunday of the national church elections (Sixth Sunday after Trinity)
sermons.published_in: DBW 12, pp. 465–470 (German); English in DBWE 12 and The Collected Sermons of Dietrich Bonhoeffer (2012), pp. 81–86
sermons.summary: Bonhoeffer notes that Jesus speaks about his church in solitude, near pagan territory and far from the crowds and the religious authorities. He contrasts people's opinions about Jesus, on which Christ will not build, with Peter's confession, which he calls revelation rather than human opinion. The church does not rest on Peter's character; Peter is weak and wavering and denies his Lord. It rests on confessing Christ: the church is to confess and proclaim, but Christ alone builds the church.
sermons.context: Preached on the day of the church elections called under Hitler, which the 'German Christians' won through pressure from local Nazi organisations. Bonhoeffer, his students and his friends, calling themselves the 'Young Reformation', had campaigned in vain for opposing candidates (Isabel Best's introduction).

sermons.title: Kirche und Völkerwelt ('The Church and the Peoples of the World')
sermons.occasion: Ecumenical conference at Fanø: introductory paper in the discussion on 'The Church and the World of Nations'
sermons.published_in: DBW 13, pp. 298–304 (German text, pp. 298–301, and an English rendering, pp. 302–304); English also in DBWE 13
sermons.summary: The address is headed by the psalm verse about God speaking peace to his people. It sets peace against the pursuit of security. It asks who can call for peace so that the world is compelled to hear, and answers that only one great ecumenical council of Christ's church from all over the world can do so, taking the weapons from its members' hands in Christ's name and forbidding them war. It asks what it might mean if a nation met an attacker praying and unarmed, and ends by pressing the urgency of the hour as the world arms itself.
sermons.context: Bonhoeffer attended as one of three international youth secretaries of the ecumenical youth commission (DBW 13 editors). The address has often been counted among his sermons and recalled as a morning devotion. The DBW 13 editors conclude from contemporary conference reports that it was a lecture, the third of four introductory papers given on 28 August 1934, and that the remembered devotion was probably a separate one on 23 August.

sermons.title: Sermons on 1 Corinthians 13 ('… and Have Not Love'; 'What Love Wants'; 'Must I Be Perfect?'; 'A Church That Believes, Hopes, and Loves')
sermons.occasion: Four consecutive Sundays: 20th–22nd Sundays after Trinity and Reformation Sunday (4 November 1934)
sermons.published_in: DBW 13, pp. 378–403 (German); English in DBWE 13 and The Collected Sermons of Dietrich Bonhoeffer (2012), pp. 139–166
sermons.summary: Over four Sundays Bonhoeffer works through Paul's chapter on love. He argues that love is in the end the one thing asked of Christians, and that a human life has meaning only insofar as love is in it. He insists that the chapter describes not what a loving person achieves but who love is: Jesus Christ, seen in the cross. Salvation therefore comes to those who have been loved, not to those who love well. The last sermon, on faith, hope and love, speaks of a love that would even give up its own salvation to bring it to others.
sermons.context: Bonhoeffer was pastor of two German-speaking congregations in London from October 1933 to April 1935. The DBW 13 editors say he preached twice each Sunday, first at the Reformed St Paul's Church in the East End and then at the united congregation in Sydenham. They add that many of his London sermon manuscripts survive because he sent them to his friend, the theologian Elisabeth Zinn.

sermons.title: The Betrayer
sermons.place: Confessing Church preachers' seminary, Finkenwalde (near Stettin)
sermons.published_in: DBW 14, pp. 973–979 (German); English in DBWE 14 and The Collected Sermons of Dietrich Bonhoeffer (2012), pp. 185–192
sermons.summary: The sermon dwells on the fact that Jesus was handed over not only by outside enemies but by one of the Twelve, a disciple he had chosen, loved and trusted. It explores the paradox of a kiss that expresses both close fellowship with Christ and betrayal of him. Even at the arrest Jesus calls Judas 'friend' and does not let him go. Bonhoeffer asks each disciple, and the church, to ask 'Lord, is it I?', and to take refuge in Christ's suffering for all sin, including betrayal, instead of condemning Judas.
sermons.context: Preached at the Confessing Church's illegal seminary at Finkenwalde on the day before its fourth course ended. According to DBW 14, that course ran from 17 October 1936 to 15 March 1937, while Bonhoeffer was working on Discipleship.

sermons.title: Predigt über einen Rachepsalm ('Sermon on a Psalm of Vengeance')
sermons.occasion: Sunday sermon during the seminary's fifth course (DBW 14 designates the day the 8th Sunday after Trinity)
sermons.published_in: Gesammelte Schriften IV, pp. 413–422; critical text DBW 14, pp. 980–988; English in DBWE 14 and, earlier, in Theology Today 38/4 (January 1982), pp. 465–471 (trans. Daniel Bloesch, ed. F. Burton Nelson)
sermons.summary: Bonhoeffer asks whether Christians may pray a psalm that calls down vengeance on the wicked. He answers that sinners cannot, because only someone without sin could pray it: Christ prays it in David, and his innocence, not ours, accuses the world. Faced with the enemies of God and the church, Christians can only pray, and those who leave vengeance to God give up their own revenge, suffer patiently and love their enemies. God's vengeance has already fallen on Christ at the cross, where he prayed for his enemies' forgiveness, so God's judgment is seen in the cross. Christians can therefore pray the psalm in gratitude, asking God to bring their enemies under the cross and show them mercy.
sermons.context: Preached during the seminary's fifth and last course (18 April – 11 September 1937), which ended with the seminary being banned (DBW 14); the Gestapo closed Finkenwalde in September 1937 (USHMM). Introducing the 1982 English translation, F. Burton Nelson links the sermon's opening reference to 'the church's distress' to the arrests of Confessing Church pastors, including Martin Niemöller on 1 July 1937, and says it was written ten days after Niemöller's arrest.

sermons.title: Loving Our Enemies
sermons.occasion: Third Sunday after Epiphany; Confessing Church collective pastorate (Sammelvikariat)
sermons.published_in: DBW 15, pp. 463–469 (German); English in DBWE 15 and The Collected Sermons of Dietrich Bonhoeffer (2012), pp. 193–200
sermons.summary: Bonhoeffer tells hearers to remember that they too were God's enemies and received mercy they did not deserve. He warns that when people trust their own judgment of good and evil, they end up devouring one another. Because Christ's cross belongs to all people, God loves enemies and suffered for them. Christians must therefore not repay evil with evil, must seek peace with everyone, and must leave vengeance to God. Caring for an enemy is the 'burning coals' that can bring repentance, and evil is overcome when it finds no answering hatred to feed on.
sermons.context: After the Gestapo closed Finkenwalde in September 1937 (USHMM), Bonhoeffer continued training ordinands in collective pastorates in Pomerania; DBW 15 places this sermon at Gross-Schlönwitz. Reviewer Thomas Baker (Commonweal) notes that it was preached in 1938 to these clandestine seminarians in East Pomerania.

sermons.title: The Peace of God in Affliction (Sermon on Romans 5:1–5)
sermons.occasion: Printed and sent to former Finkenwalde seminarians
sermons.published_in: DBW 15, pp. 470–475 (German); English in DBWE 15 and The Collected Sermons of Dietrich Bonhoeffer, vol. 2 (2017)
sermons.summary: Peace with God comes only through Christ's cross, where God's wrath was borne and reconciliation was made, and it requires giving up one's own will. Whether this peace is real shows in how Christians meet affliction: those who speak highly of the cross but avoid hardship have no peace with God. For those who love God, suffering produces patience, patience produces tested experience, and experience produces hope. Turning away from God's peace leads instead from affliction to impatience, hardening and despair, a reversed chain Bonhoeffer quotes from Luther.
sermons.context: Written after the Gestapo closed the Finkenwalde seminary in September 1937 (USHMM). Reviewer Kyle Jantzen reports that it was printed and sent to the now scattered Finkenwalde seminarians to encourage them.

sources.label: Kyle Jantzen, review of Collected Sermons vol. 2, Contemporary Church History Quarterly (2018)

sermons.title: Death Is Swallowed Up in Victory
sermons.occasion: Communion address on Totensonntag (Sunday of remembrance of the dead) for the remaining seminarians
sermons.published_in: DBW 15, pp. 488–490 (German); English in DBWE 15 and The Collected Sermons of Dietrich Bonhoeffer (2012), pp. 207–210
sermons.summary: Given at a communion service on the Sunday when the dead are remembered, the address takes up Paul's cry of triumph over death. It proclaims Christ's victory over death as something the church preaches and believes in spite of what it sees: the graves of loved ones, the dying of nature in late autumn, and the death the war was once again bringing. While the reign of death is visible, the address holds that Christ's victory over it is what the church believes.
sermons.context: Given a few months after the Second World War began, at a communion service with Bonhoeffer's remaining seminarians (reviewer Barry Harvey). DBW 15 places it at Sigurdshof, where the collective pastorate was then based. It is the last sermon in Isabel Best's collection.

sermons.title: Lazarus and the Rich Man
sermons.date_text: 29 May 1932 (date marked uncertain by the German editors)
sermons.published_in: DBW 11, pp. 426–434 (German); English in DBWE 11 and The Collected Sermons of Dietrich Bonhoeffer (2012), pp. 33–40
sermons.summary: Bonhoeffer argues that the parable is usually reduced to a moral lesson that the rich should help the poor, and that it is in fact a much harder text. He says it confronts hearers with their disdain for the poor and wretched, and with their reluctance to accept that such people are their equals in God's eyes.
sermons.context: Preached in Berlin in 1932, when Bonhoeffer was also teaching a confirmation class at Zion Church in working-class north Berlin (Isabel Best's introduction). DBW 11 dates it to the First Sunday after Trinity, 29 May 1932, with a question mark.
